summary:
The Falkland Islands are a British Overseas Territory with their own Legislative Assembly, which legislates locally. Same-sex activity has been legal since 1989, and the age of consent has been equal since 2005.

Same-sex marriage and civil partnerships have been available since 29 April 2017. The Legislative Assembly passed the bill in March 2017 by 7 votes to 1, and the registrar general confirmed by reply in June 2017 that it is law. Civil partnerships are open to opposite-sex couples as well as same-sex couples. A public consultation preceding the bill showed 90% support for same-sex marriage and 94% for civil partnerships in a territory of roughly 3,000 residents.

Stepchild and joint adoption have been available to same-sex couples since 2017.

The Constitution Order 2008, at Article 16, bans discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation. The sources identify sexual orientation only; no gender-identity ground is stated in the Constitution.

United Kingdom frameworks do not reach the Islands. The UK Equality Act 2010 and the Gender Recognition Act 2004 do not extend to the Falkland Islands, so protection and recognition depend on the territory's own ordinances.

Legal gender change has been possible since 2014 under the CPE Ordinance 2014. There is no self-identification route and no recognition of non-binary status, and holders of a UK Gender Recognition Certificate are recognised in their acquired gender under that ordinance.

Three ordinances frame the criminal-justice treatment of bias. The Crimes Ordinance 2014 provides for hate-stirring on grounds of sexual orientation, the CPE Ordinance 2014 provides for sexual orientation as an aggravating factor in sentencing, and a Prisons Ordinance was enacted in 2017.

The United Kingdom is responsible for the territory's defence.
tangentialFactors:
The same registrar general who confirmed the marriage law also confirmed that same-sex marriage is not legal in the South Georgia and South Sandwich Islands dependency, so the equality reform does not extend to that associated territory.

Public attitudes are reported as largely positive, consistent with the 90% consultation support for same-sex marriage recorded before the 2017 bill.
localsOnly:
Residents access gender recognition and bias-motivated-crime protections through the territory's own ordinances rather than UK statute, since the Equality Act 2010 and Gender Recognition Act 2004 do not extend to the Islands.

Civil partnerships are available to opposite-sex couples as well as same-sex couples, so the 2017 reform is not limited to same-sex relationships.
outOfScopeNotes:
The sources do not state whether the Constitution's sexual-orientation discrimination ban has been litigated or how it is enforced in practice; enforcement outcomes remain unresolved.

No source in the inventory addresses transgender-specific violence, hate-crime incident data, or facility and restroom access on the Islands; those questions are not sourced here.

The inventory does not indicate whether the Crimes Ordinance 2014 hate-stirring provision or the CPE Ordinance 2014 sentencing aggravation has been applied in any recorded case.
